title: Social Media and the End of Higher Ed
author: Dempsey, Patrick
summary: Patrick Dempsey uses Arizona State University's new Bachelor of Arts in Content Creation as a case study in why traditional higher education is fundamentally misaligned with the creator economy. The programme's core failures are credibility (professors aren't successful creators), curriculum lag (by the time a course reaches the catalogue the platform may be obsolete), and value proposition (students pay four years of tuition for roughly twelve credit hours of actual content creation instruction, while the creator economy delivers direct learning from practitioners).
points: Credibility is the fatal flaw: teaching someone to become a successful creator requires being a successful creator—no theoretical framework substitutes for demonstrated practice in a fast-moving field.
The creator economy moves at platform speed; by the time a university proposes, approves, designs, builds, catalogues, and schedules a course, the platform it teaches may be unrecognisable.
ASU's 120-credit degree dedicates only 12 credit hours to explicitly designated content creation work—the rest is traditional journalism and communications coursework.
The fundamental value proposition of creator education is learning directly from someone already doing it—which is what the creator economy delivers and universities structurally cannot.
The university model retains value for stable, foundational disciplines resistant to rapid obsolescence; content creation is none of these things.
quotes: (Do they even know what Skool and Circle are?) But the way the creator economy works today is that you give all your content away for free and then teach that same content at increasingly higher prices in exchange for increased access to the successful creator.

ASU lists 57 hours of major requirements, but much of that will likely be standard journalism and mass communication coursework: grammar, media writing, information gathering, media ethics, media law, visual communication, and media organizations.

Meanwhile, a university has to propose the course, get the course approved by some external governing body, design the course, build the course, get the course into the catalog, assign the course, and schedule the course .

And maybe there is a sense in which you think, “Well, I don’t know who Kallaway is, but you seem to have more information than I have, so I’d be willing to pay you to help me get better at posting on LinkedIn.” For sure.

ASU’s promise is that its program will prepare students to “become an influencer and strategic storyteller.” “prepare to become.” And right here is the problem with this program and every program institutions offer.

So, let’s be clear about what is happening here: Students pursuing a four-year degree in content creation are guaranteed about four courses specifically designated for content-creation skills and practice.
